section.content: The present application relates to an Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) tensor processor. A system for performing tensor operations comprising: a programmable tensor processor; and a memory coupled to the programmable tensor processor, wherein the programmable tensor processor includes: one or more load AGU circuits that generate a first address sequence and read input tensor operands from the memory based on the first address sequence; a data path circuit that performs the tensor operation on the input tensor operand based on receiving one or more instructions that determine the output tensor operand, the one or more instructions based on a loop iteration count and a loop body microcode instruction that defines a loop body of a tensor program stored in the memory, the loop body microcode instruction executing in the programmable tensor processor; and a storage AGU circuit configured to generate a second sequence of addresses and to write the output tensor operand to the memory based on the second sequence of addresses.

本申请涉及人工智能(AI)/机器学习(ML)张量处理器。一种用于执行张量操作的系统包含：可编程张量处理器；以及存储器，其耦合到所述可编程张量处理器，其中所述可编程张量处理器包含：一或多个加载AGU电路，其产生第一地址序列并且基于所述第一地址序列从所述存储器读取输入张量操作数；数据路径电路，其基于接收到确定输出张量操作数的一或多个指令而对所述输入张量操作数执行所述张量操作，所述一或多个指令基于环路迭代计数和环路主体微码指令，所述环路主体微码指令定义存储于所述存储器中的张量程序的环路主体，所述环路主体微码指令在所述可编程张量处理器中执行；以及存储AGU电路，其被配置成产生第二地址序列并且基于所述第二地址序列，将所述输出张量操作数写入到所述存储器。

Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) tensor processorRELATED APPLICATIONS

The present application claims priority and benefit from U.S. provisional patent application No. 63/346,204, filed in the U.S. patent and trademark office at 5.26, 2022, the entire contents of which are incorporated herein by reference.

Technical Field

The present application relates generally to an Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) tensor processor. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to systems and methods for providing tensor operations using an AI/ML tensor processor.

Background

Tensors can be used to describe physical properties, similar to scalar and vector De mathematic objects. Tensors can be considered as generalizations of scalar and vector. For example, the scalar is a zero rank tensor and the vector is a rank tensor. The tensors may be used to represent inputs, outputs, and transforms within the neural network, and as such, the neural network regularly operates with the tensors. For example, tensors may be the primary data structure for use by the neural network, such as for storing weights for connections between layers of the neural network, as well as for storing values propagated through the neural network.

The above information in the background section is only for enhancement of understanding of the background of the technology and therefore should not be construed as an admission that the prior art exists or is relevant.

Disclosure of Invention

This summary is provided to introduce a selection of features and concepts of embodiments of the disclosure that are further described below in the detailed description. This summary is not intended to identify key or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to be used to limit the scope of the claimed subject matter. One or more of the described features may be combined with one or more other described features to provide a workable device.

In one or more embodiments, a system for performing tensor operations, the system comprising: a programmable tensor processor; and a memory coupled to the programmable tensor processor, wherein the programmable tensor processor includes: one or more load Address Generation Unit (AGU) circuits configured to generate a first address sequence and read input tensor operands from the memory based on the first address sequence; a data path circuit configured to perform the tensor operation on the input tensor operand based on receiving one or more instructions to determine an output tensor operand, the one or more instructions based on a loop iteration count and a loop body microcode instruction defining a loop body of a tensor program stored in the memory, the loop body microcode instruction executing in the programmable tensor processor; and a storage AGU circuit configured to generate a second sequence of addresses and to write the output tensor operand to the memory based on the second sequence of addresses.

In one or more embodiments, the one or more load AGU circuits are configured to generate the first address sequence based on receipt of one or more input address generation parameters based on the tensor program stored in the memory, and to generate the second address sequence based on receipt of one or more output address generation parameters based on the tensor program stored in the memory.

In one or more embodiments, the tensor operation includes one or more selected from the group of arithmetic operations, look-up table (LUT) based operations, multiply and multiply-accumulate operations, transpose and shuffle operations, and/or reduction operations.

In one or more embodiments, the tensor program is decomposed into an input operand memory load section, a loop sequencing section, a loop body microcode execution across functional circuitry of the datapath circuitry, and an output operand memory storage section, wherein the loop sequencing section of the tensor program includes the loop iteration count of the tensor program and a plurality of predicate instructions representing the loop body microcode instructions, and wherein the loop iteration count is a set of values.

In one or more embodiments, the first address sequence is generated based on the input operand memory load section of the tensor program and the second address sequence is generated based on the output operand memory store section of the tensor program.

In one or more embodiments, the programmable tensor processor further includes: a nested loop sequence circuit configured to iterate loops in the tensor program based on the loop iteration count of the tensor program and generate a conditional code stream; an predicate filter circuit configured to filter a subset of the loop body microcode instructions based on the condition code stream from the nested loop sequencer circuit and to generate filtered instructions containing corresponding predicate instructions; and a pending instruction tracker circuit configured to track the filtered instructions in an instruction queue from the predicate filter circuit and issue the one or more instructions in the filtered instructions to the data path circuit, the one or more instructions being at a head of the instruction queue.

In one or more embodiments, the predicate filter circuit is configured to filter one or more instructions from the loop body microcode instructions that fail a conditional check based on the condition code stream received from the nested loop sequencer circuit.

In one or more embodiments, the pending instruction tracker circuit is further configured to maintain a schedule instruction table including the instruction queue, shift the schedule instruction table to remove the one or more instructions after the one or more instructions from the head of the instruction queue are issued to the data path circuit, and accept and add a new iteration of the filtered instructions to the schedule instruction table, wherein the new iteration of the filtered instructions added to the schedule instruction table is not dangerous.

In one or more embodiments, the data path circuit includes: one or more load function circuits configured to load the input tensor operand through the one or more load AGU circuits; one or more arithmetic logic function circuits configured to perform the tensor operation; one or more multiplier function circuits; at least one storage circuit configured to store the output tensor operand and store an intermediate result of the tensor operation by the storage AGU circuit; and at least one register file circuit storing intermediate results of the tensor operation.

In one or more embodiments, a method for performing tensor operations in a neural network, the method comprising: generating, by a processor, a first address sequence; reading, by the processor, an input tensor operand from a memory coupled to the processor based on the first sequence of addresses; iterating, by the processor, loops in a tensor program stored in the memory and generating a conditional code stream; filtering, by the processor, a subset of microcode instructions from loop body microcode instructions of the tensor program based on the condition code stream, and generating filtered instructions; performing, by the processor, the tensor operation on the input tensor operand based on one or more instructions of the filtered instructions to determine an output tensor operand; generating, by the processor, a second sequence of addresses; and writing, by the processor, the output tensor operand to the memory based on the second sequence of addresses.

In one or more embodiments, the method further comprises: tracking, by the processor, the filtered instructions in an instruction queue; and data path circuitry to issue the one or more instructions to the processor by the processor, the one or more instructions being at a head of the instruction queue.

In one or more embodiments, the method further comprises: maintaining, by the processor, a scheduling instruction table containing the instruction queue; and shifting, by the processor, the table to remove the one or more instructions after the one or more instructions from the head of the instruction queue are issued to the data path circuitry; and accepting, by the processor, a new iteration of the filtered instruction and adding the new iteration of the filtered instruction to the schedule instruction table, wherein the new iteration of the filtered instruction added to the schedule instruction table is not dangerous.

In one or more embodiments, the processor is configured to iterate the loop in the tensor program based on a loop iteration count of the tensor program, wherein the loop body microcode instructions define a loop body of the tensor program and execute in the processor, wherein the filtered instructions include a plurality of predicate instructions representing the subset of the microcode instructions after filtering, and wherein two or more predicate instructions from among the plurality of predicate instructions are allocated to a same functional circuit at a same loop based on predicate mutual exclusion in the two or more predicate instructions.

In one or more embodiments, the first address sequence is generated based on the tensor program based on receiving one or more input address generation parameters, and wherein the second address sequence is generated based on the tensor program based on receiving one or more output address generation parameters.

In one or more embodiments, the tensor operation includes one or more selected from the group of arithmetic operations, look-up table (LUT) based operations, multiply and multiply-accumulate operations, transpose and shuffle operations, and/or reduction operations.

In one or more embodiments, a non-transitory computer-readable medium comprising stored instructions that, when executed by a processor, cause the processor to generate a digital representation of a tensor processor circuit comprising: one or more load Address Generation Unit (AGU) circuits configured to generate a first address sequence and read input tensor operands from a memory coupled to the tensor processor circuit based on the first address sequence; a data path circuit configured to perform a tensor operation on an input tensor operand based on receiving one or more instructions to determine the output tensor operand, the one or more instructions based on a loop iteration count and a loop body microcode instruction defining a loop body of a tensor program stored in the memory, the loop body microcode instruction executing in the programmable tensor processor; and a storage AGU circuit configured to generate a second sequence of addresses and to write the output tensor operand to the memory based on the second sequence of addresses.

In one or more embodiments, the non-transitory computer-readable medium of claim 16 wherein the tensor processor circuit further includes: a nested loop sequence circuit configured to iterate loops in the tensor program based on the loop iteration count of the tensor program and generate a conditional code stream; an predicate filter circuit configured to filter a subset of the loop body microcode instructions based on the condition code stream from the nested loop sequencer circuit and to generate filtered instructions containing corresponding predicate instructions; and a pending instruction tracker circuit configured to track the filtered instructions in an instruction queue from the predicate filter circuit and issue the one or more instructions in the filtered instructions to the data path circuit, the one or more instructions being at a head of the instruction queue.

In one or more embodiments, the data path circuit includes: one or more load function circuits configured to load the input tensor operand through the one or more load AGU circuits; one or more arithmetic logic function circuits configured to perform the tensor operation; at least one storage circuit configured to store the output tensor operand and store an intermediate result of the tensor operation by the storage AGU circuit; and at least one register file circuit storing intermediate results of the tensor operation.

In one or more embodiments, the tensor program is decomposed into an input operand memory load section, a loop sequencing section, a loop body section that executes across functional units, and an output operand memory store section, wherein the loop sequencing section of the tensor program includes the loop iteration count of the tensor program and a plurality of predicate instructions that represent the loop body microcode instructions, and wherein the loop iteration count is a set of values.

In one or more embodiments, the tensor operation includes one or more selected from the group of arithmetic operations, look-up table (LUT) based operations, multiply and multiply-accumulate operations, transpose and shuffle operations, and/or reduction operations.

Detailed Description

Aspects of the present disclosure relate to an Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) tensor processor.

State-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) applications rely on vector, matrix and tensor operations. To process data through an artificial Neural Network (NN), the architecture of the artificial neural network may be converted into an intermediate primitive form. In ML, a primitive may also be the smallest processing unit available to a programmer of a particular machine, or may be an atomic element of an expression in a language. These primitives may represent basic calculations such as tensor addition, tensor multiplication, activation functions (e.g., parameter correction linear units or PReLUs), and so forth. These primitives may be optimized for computation on some given hardware and once implemented, may be reused or referenced by additional models.

For example, different activation functions of an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) may be represented by different sets of primitive comparison and selection operations. In ANN, the normalization layer may require yet another set of primitive operations. Moreover, through academic research, new operation types are continually emerging (e.g., different activation functions and different types of neural network layers).

The AI/ML application or ANN includes a layer of functions. The inputs and outputs of layers of an ANN may be expressed as tensors (e.g., matrices, vectors, and scalars are tensor subsets). Additionally, a layer may include trainable parameters (e.g., weights) whose values are set during the process of training the ANN, and the parameters of a given layer may also be expressed as tensors. In ML, tensors are a way to embed high-dimensional data into a multidimensional array (e.g., data type) that is suitable for ANN. Tensors may represent images, movies, volumes, sounds, and relationships among words and concepts in a unified manner (e.g., as a series of values that may be organized along n different dimensions).

Various AI layer functions (e.g., activation functions, normalization, etc.) may be expressed using a common Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) in which a plurality of instructions form a program (e.g., a computer program). The ISA may represent instructions supported by the AI processor. In such cases, flexibility may be desirable because new function types continue to emerge through academic research, and ISA may allow AI processors to implement these new types of functions.

High throughput may be desirable in AI processors, and thus, AI processors use Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) processing data vectors (or tensors) and Very Large Instruction Words (VLIWs), issuing a bundle of instructions across multiple functional units, one instruction per unit per cycle. In AI tensor operation, the instruction program stream may not depend on the tensor value (i.e., the program control stream will not depend on the data value), and the memory access sequence is known in advance.

In AI/ML applications (e.g., using computer Software (SW)), primitive tensor operations may be expressed by a single nested 'for' loop set. When multiple primitive operations are combined into a sequence (e.g., a computer program), the 'if-then-else' statement provides conditional execution of the primitive operation. For example, a tensor program (e.g., representing a neural network) may include one or more input tensor operands and, as a result of its tensor processing, generate one or more tensor output operands. Operations on tensors are characterized as a set of nested loops and loop bodies to be executed, and 'if-then-else' can be used to control the 'for' loop (e.g., using the 'if' statement to detect when the for loop completes an iteration of the dimension of the input tensor).

Many modern computer processors have a deep instruction pipeline in which instructions are queued for execution. A conditional statement (e.g., an 'if' statement) is typically represented in the ISA of a processor as a conditional branch or conditional branch instruction, where the next instruction to be executed by the processor depends on the outcome of an evaluation condition (e.g., an instruction that executes branch a if the condition is true and an instruction that executes branch B if the condition is false). Because the next instruction to be executed must not be known before the processor evaluates the condition, the processor must wait until the condition is executed (leaving the instruction pipeline empty and thereby wasting computation cycles before waiting for the determined next instruction to be retrieved from memory and inserted into the queue), or the processor may assert or guess which branch to take (in which case, in the case of an incorrect assertion by the processor's branch asserting circuit, effort may be wasted).

In one or more embodiments of the present disclosure, a multi-level nested loop body is reconstructed (or decomposed) to use multi-level assertions. This avoids the use of conditional statements (or 'if' statements) in the loop, thereby increasing the throughput of the AI tensor processor according to embodiments of the present disclosure. In computer architecture, assertions are a feature that provides an alternative to conditional branching of control, as implemented by conditional branch machine instructions. An predicate works by associating conditional (e.g., predicated) non-branch instructions with the predicate, which is a boolean value that is used by the instruction to control whether the instruction is allowed to modify the architectural state. For example, an assertion is a statement (or function) that returns true or false. If the assertion specified in the instruction is true, the instruction modifies the architectural state; otherwise, the architecture state is unchanged. For example, the predicated move instruction (conditional move) only modifies the destination if the predicate is true. Thus, instead of using conditional branches to select an instruction or sequence of instructions to execute based on an assertion that controls whether the branch occurs (e.g., by jumping to another portion of the program based on an evaluation of the assertion), an instruction to be executed is associated with that assertion such that the instruction to be executed is executed or not based on whether the assertion is true or false. Regardless of whether the predicate of the predicate instruction is true or false, after executing the predicate instruction, the processor continues to execute the next instruction of the program (e.g., the predicate instruction does not cause a jump). In one or more embodiments, assertions may depend on, for example, nested loop (e.g., nested "for" loops) variables (e.g., first or last or odd or even in inner or outer loops).

One or more embodiments of the present disclosure provide a processor (e.g., a tensor processor) or programmable tensor processor that speeds up AI/ML tensor-based operations while maintaining flexibility as found in other programmable solutions. The programmable processor or programmable tensor processor may also provide flexibility to support various operations (e.g., tensor operations, neural network layers, activation functions, etc.) now and in the future, as new operation types emerge over time.

Technical advantages of the present disclosure include, but are not limited to, efficient, low area, high throughput hardware, or a programmable tensor processor for performing efficient flexible tensor operation acceleration, such as for use in implementing a Neural Network (NN), such as would be used in an edge reasoning processor. For example, to efficiently perform tensor operations in an NN, one or more embodiments of the present disclosure provide a programmable tensor processor in which a Software (SW) program is broken down into at least four functions (e.g., load/store, address generation, loop sequencing, predicate filtering, computation, etc.). The SW program is executed by mapping the components of the SW program on the modules using a streaming paradigm for communication between the modules. The loop structure of the SW program is predefined. In a programmable tensor processor according to some embodiments, microcode of the SW program is explicitly scheduled by the compiler, there is no conflict with a single iteration of the inner loop of the SW program, and thus no intra-iteration body hazards (e.g., no resource conflicts, e.g., no read-after-register hazards, and no functional unit allocation conflicts). The microcode program may define the inner loop body of the SW program to be executed in each inner loop iteration in the programmable tensor processor.

Technical advantages of the present disclosure also include pipelining the reading of new programs and the execution of current programs. In addition, the programmable tensor processor of the present disclosure provides fully predicable execution of tensor operations (e.g., without the need to evaluate conditional branch instructions). For example, because in the programmable tensor processor of the present disclosure there is no need to evaluate conditional branch instructions (e.g., predicate statements eliminate the need for branch predicates), the programmable tensor processor of the present disclosure may occupy less area in an Integrated Circuit (IC) and consume less power.

In one or more embodiments of the present disclosure, a subset of instructions to enable in the loop body is asserted. In one or more embodiments, assertions depend only on nested loop variables (e.g., first/last/even/odd on outer/middle/inner loops). In another embodiment, the mutex predicate may enable different instructions on the same slot.

In one or more embodiments, the decomposed SW program may be executed on a device (e.g., a processor (e.g., a tensor processor)) having a similar decomposition structure, where devices (e.g., circuits) communicate using a streaming paradigm.

FIG. 1 illustrates building blocks representing an exploded version of a tensor operation on two tensors in an ANN.

As shown in the data flow of the tensor processor 100 of fig. 1, the two input tensors (in 0 and in 1) may be stored in one or more locations of the memory 102 in communication with the tensor processor 100. In one or more embodiments of the present disclosure, the program flow or control flow is independent of the values in the input tensors in0, in 1. In other words, the control flow is independent of the data flow.

In one or more embodiments, when an input address generation parameter instruction 112 is received at one or more load Address Generation Unit (AGU) circuits 104 (1) and 104 (2), the two load AGU circuits 104 (1) and 104 (2) may read data from the memory 102 (1), 102 (2)) and stream the data to the compute or data path circuit 106. The data path circuitry 106 performs calculations on the input tensors (in 0 and in 1) based on one or more instructions received at the data path circuitry 106. The data path circuitry 106 forwards the result of the computation to the storage AGU circuitry 108. The storage AGU circuit 108 can receive the output address generation parameter instruction 114 and based on receiving the output address generation parameter instruction 114, the storage AGU circuit 108 can write the results to one or more locations 110 of a memory (e.g., memory 102). For example, in this case, the 'body' in the data path circuitry 106 specifies one or more operations (e.g., tensor operations, such as arithmetic operations) to be performed on the input tensors (in 0 and in 1), and the data path circuitry 106 may perform the operations only when the input tensors (in 0 and in 1) data are available (e.g., from the two loading AGU circuits 104 (1) and 104 (2)). The parameters of these functions are known a priori, e.g. designated as part of the program being executed, set statically at the time of compiling the program or set dynamically when the program is initially run.

Fig. 2-4 provide examples of tensor operations in AI/ML. Fig. 2 illustrates pseudo code of a tensor 'add' operation on two tensors, fig. 3 illustrates building blocks representing an exploded version of the tensor operation on two tensors of fig. 2, and fig. 4 illustrates another embodiment of an exploded version of the pseudo code of fig. 2.

As discussed above, the AI function operates on tensor operands. Each tensor has a rank, which is the number of dimensions in the tensor data. The C pseudo code of fig. 2 illustrates the tensor 'add' operation on two tensors (in 0 and in 1) of unequal ranks 2 and 1. The addition operation on the tensors produces a tensor (output) of rank 2.

For example, in FIG. 2, the program flow does not depend on the values in tensors in0 and in1 (the control flow is independent of the data or data flow). The loop boundaries are pre-known based on the tensor dimension (in 0 is the tensor of rank 2 with dimensions 3 and 4 and in1 is the tensor of rank 1 with dimension 3, and thus i iterates 3 times; j iterates 3 x 4 times)), and the memory access sequence (e.g., the load/store is also pre-known (e.g., [ i ] [ j ], 3 x [ i ]). Given the above observations, a program such as that shown in FIG. 2 may be broken down into separate streams of functions (e.g., 118, 120, 122, and 124) as illustrated in FIG. 3.

In the example embodiment of fig. 3, the two input tensors (in 0 and in 1) may be stored in one or more locations of the memory 102. In one or more embodiments of the present disclosure, the program or control flow (represented in FIG. 3 by instructions 118, 120, 122, and 124 and the pending instruction tracker circuit 116) is independent of the values in the input tensors (in 0, in 1). In other words, the control flow is independent of the data flow. In fig. 3, the data flow is represented by the memory 102 (102 (1), 102 (2)), the one or more load AGU circuits 104 (104 (1), 104 (2)), the data path circuit 106, the store AGU circuit 108, and the one or more locations 110 of the memory (e.g., memory 102), and the program flow or control flow may be represented by the instructions 118, 120, 122, and 124 and the pending instruction tracker circuit 116.

In one or more embodiments in FIG. 3, when a load AGU parameter instruction 118 (e.g., that is part of a control flow) is received at the load AGU circuits 104 (1) and 104 (2), the two load AGU circuits 104 (1) and 104 (2) may read data (in 0[ i ] [ j ], in1[ i ]) from the memory 102 (1), 102 (2)) and stream the data to the data path circuit 106. The data path circuitry 106 performs calculations on the input tensors (in 0[ i ] [ j ], in1[ i ]) based on one or more instructions received at the data path circuitry 106. For example, the pending instruction tracker circuit 116 may receive a loop parameter instruction 120 and a data path parameter instruction 122 (e.g., microcode for a loop body), and based on the loop parameter instruction 120 and the data path parameter instruction 122, the pending instruction tracker circuit 116 may issue a bundle of instructions into the data path circuit 106, one instruction from the bundle of instructions per functional unit per loop iteration. For example, in this case, the 'body' (e.g., the datapath parameter instruction 122 or microcode for the loop body) may specify a tensor operation (e.g., arithmetic operation) to be performed on the data (in 0[ i ] [ j ], in1[ i ]) and may be performed only when the input data is available. The parameters of these functions are known a priori (e.g., based on the dimensions of the input).

The data path circuitry 106 forwards the result of the computation to the storage AGU circuitry 108. The storage AGU circuit 108 can receive an output address generation parameter instruction 114 (e.g., that is part of a control flow) and based on receiving the output address generation parameter instruction 114, the storage AGU circuit 108 can write the results to one or more locations 110 of a memory (e.g., memory 102).

As shown in the pseudo-code of fig. 2 and 4, the first input tensor "in0" is a tensor of rank 2 of the integer data type having dimensions 3 and 4, the second input tensor "in1" is a tensor of rank 1 of the integer data type having dimensions 3, and the output tensor "output" represents a result of a tensor operation (e.g., an arithmetic operation, such as "addition") between the first input tensor "in0" and the second input tensor "in1" is a tensor of rank 2 of the integer data type having dimensions 3 and 4. The first input tensor "in0" and the second input tensor "in1" may be loaded from the memory 102 for storage in the scratch pad register.

In the pseudo code of fig. 2, the tensor operation (e.g., the "add" operation) between the first input tensor "in0" and the second input tensor "in1" may be expressed by a single nested 'for' loop set. In the example of FIG. 2, each "in1" value is referenced four times. The valid solution may load each value from memory 102 (102 (1), 102 (2)) only once and store it into a scratch pad register, as shown in fig. 4. In one or more embodiments, a microcode program defining the inner loop body will be executed at each inner loop iteration. The subset of instructions executed may be defined by a set of condition codes that depend on the nested loop iteration count.

Fig. 5A illustrates a tensor program including input tensor operands.

For example, in general, a tensor program includes an input tensor operand, a loop set (e.g., "for loop"), a condition (e.g., "if-the else" condition), and a body as illustrated in fig. 5A. The body may contain one or more instructions from the ISA. As discussed above, various AI layer functions (e.g., activation functions, normalization, etc.) may be expressed using an ISA in which a plurality of instructions form a program (e.g., a computer program). In the tensor procedure, 'if-the-else' refers only to the loop counter, compared to the start or end condition of the loop. In one or more embodiments, the loop counter may be a counter maintained by a "datapath" circuit of the programmable tensor processor. The loop counter may be incremented at the end of each loop iteration. In one or more embodiments, a separate counter is maintained for each (nested) loop that is incremented at the end of each loop iteration. For example, in fig. 5A, the condition of execution of the "subject 3" is the same as the condition of execution of the "subject 6". In fig. 5A, the right example illustrates how AI 'sum pooling' operations may be mapped on the loop structure on the left side of fig. 5A (e.g., where a particular operation is mapped onto a "body" placeholder).

The procedure as shown in fig. 5A may be transformed into a procedure in which all if-the-else bodies move into the inner loop, as illustrated in fig. 5B.

For example, FIG. 5B illustrates a program in which all if-the-else bodies of FIG. 5A move into an inner loop, and FIG. 5C illustrates a program in which each row of FIG. 5B containing an incorporated "if" statement is mapped onto an predicate instruction.

FIG. 7A illustrates a programmable tensor processor (or streaming tensor processor) in accordance with one or more embodiments. FIG. 7B illustrates an example data path of the programmable tensor processor of FIG. 7A.

The programmable tensor processor 700 provides efficient and flexible tensor operation acceleration.

The programmable tensor processor 700 includes load AGU circuitry (704 (1), 704 (2)), data path circuitry 706, store AGU circuitry (e.g., 708), nested loop sequencer circuitry 712, predicate filter circuitry 714, and pending instruction tracker circuitry 718.

The load AGU circuits 704 (1), 704 (2)) may read data from the memories 702 (1) and 702 (2), and the store AGU circuit 708 may store the results of the computation or the output of the data path circuit 706 in another memory 710. In the programmable tensor processor 700 of the present application, a plurality of circuits (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2), 706, 708, 712, 714, 718) are connected via a streaming interface (e.g., a data streaming protocol, such as a point-to-point communication protocol for communicating data from an initiator port to a target port).

In the programmable tensor processor 700 of the present disclosure, the SW program is broken down into multiple sections, such as an input operand memory loading section (e.g., performed by the loading AGU circuits 704 (1), 704 (2) of fig. 1), a loop sequencing section (e.g., performed by the nested loop sequencer circuit 712, the predicate filter circuit 714, and the pending instruction tracker circuit 718), a loop body execution section across functional units (e.g., performed by the data path circuit 706), and an output operand memory storage section (e.g., performed by the storage AGU circuit 708).

FIG. 8 illustrates an example of a tensor program broken into multiple segments. The tensor program may be stored in a memory in communication with the programmable tensor processor 700 and may be executed in the programmable tensor processor 700. In particular, the tensor program may be broken down into four segments, e.g., may be represented as a C data structure, as shown in FIG. 8. For example, a tensor program may be broken down into an input operand memory load section, a loop sequencing section, a loop body execution section across functional units, and an output operand memory store section. In one or more embodiments, the programmable tensor processor 700 performs the SW program of fig. 8 by executing components of the SW program on corresponding Hardware (HW) devices or sub-circuits of the programmable tensor processor, using communication between these circuits in a point-to-point streaming paradigm. For example, in one or more embodiments, programmable tensor processor 700 may include at least four components, such as tensor input operand loading circuitry (e.g., including loading AGU circuitry 704 (1), 704 (2)), loop sequencing circuitry (e.g., including nested loop sequencer circuitry 712, predicate filter circuitry 714, and pending instruction tracker circuitry 718), loop body execution circuitry (e.g., including data path circuitry 706), and tensor output operand storage circuitry (e.g., including storage AGU circuitry 708) to execute a tensor SW program that is broken down into four functions.

In one or more embodiments, the data structure of FIG. 8 may be stored as descriptors in memory (e.g., 702, 708) and/or one or more registers. In one or more embodiments, the descriptor may have a next field to create a descriptor list. In one or more embodiments, the programmable tensor processor 700 may have two or more register sets such that the programmable tensor processor 700 may perform computations based on one descriptor while another descriptor is being initialized through a control process or Direct Memory Access (DMA). The fields in the tensor program of fig. 8 are passed to the individual processor circuits (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2), 706, 708, 712, 714, 718) and control the behavior of the circuits.

Returning now to fig. 7A, the programmable tensor processor 700 will be described in further detail below.

In one or more embodiments, programmable tensor processor 700 may control descriptor DMA and/or register interfaces, such as load/store address sequences (e.g., 730, 732), loop iteration count (720), and loop body microcode (724). The descriptor may be loaded by the descriptor DMA and/or software of the programming register interface, thereby initializing the values of the load/store address sequence (e.g., 730, 732), loop iteration count (720), and loop body microcode (724).

The loading AGU circuit (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2)) of the programmable tensor processor 700 is configured to generate a sequence of addresses and read the input tensor operands from the memory (e.g., 702 (1), 702 (2)) corresponding to the generated sequence of addresses. In this case, the address sequence is controlled by the inputs agu [ ] field from the tensor program of FIG. 8 (e.g., which is part of the input operand memory load section of the tensor program). For example, in one or more embodiments, based on receiving the input_ AGU [ ] address generation parameter 730, the loading AGU circuit (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2)) of the programmable tensor processor 700 generates an address sequence and reads data of an input tensor from a memory (e.g., 702 (1), 702 (2)) corresponding to the generated address sequence (e.g., reads data of the input tensor from the memory).

The storage AGU circuit (e.g., 708) of the programmable tensor processor 700 is configured to generate a sequence of addresses and write the output tensor operand to the memory (e.g., 710). In this case, the address sequence is controlled by the output_ agu [ ] field from the tensor program of FIG. 8 (which is part of the output operand memory storage section of the tensor program). For example, in one or more embodiments, based on receiving the output_ AGU [ ] address generation parameter 732, the storage AGU circuit 708 of the programmable tensor processor 700 generates a sequence of addresses and writes output data to an allocated tensor in memory corresponding to the generated sequence of addresses.

The nested loop sequencer circuit 712 of the programmable tensor processor 700 iterates through loops in the program and generates a stream of condition codes 722 (e.g., one condition code per inner loop iteration). In this case, the loop sequence is controlled by the loop_interfaces [ ] array in the tensor program of FIG. 8. For example, the nested loop sequencer circuit 712 of the programmable tensor processor 700 reads the loop iteration count 720, generating a condition code sequence 722, with a set of condition codes per loop iteration within the loop iteration count 720.

In one or more embodiments, the number of nested loops is predefined in the programmable tensor processor 700. For example, in the programmable tensor processor 700, in an N-level loop (e.g., n=3), a loop iteration count (e.g., loop iteration count 720) is predefined in a program (e.g., tensor program). In such cases, each loop level has an associated first/nfirst, last/nlast assertion (e.g., first0, first1, first2, last0, last1, last2, etc.), and all data operations are expressed as predicate instructions of the inner loop body of the tensor program. In one or more embodiments, the loop iteration count has a set or predefined value (e.g., a programmable value).

Assertion filtering circuitry 714 of programmable tensor processor 700 reads loop body microcode 724 and filters a subset of microcode instructions from loop body microcode 724 based on condition code 722 from loop sequencer circuitry 712. Microcode instructions or loop body microcode 724 may be represented in equivalent predicate instructions. In this case, unfiltered microcode (e.g., loop body microcode 724) is specified in the inner_body [ ] field of the tensor program of fig. 8. Predicate filter circuit 714 processes loop body microcode 724 and passes filtered instructions (e.g., predicate microcode 726) to pending instruction tracker circuit 718. For example, predicate filter circuit 714 of programmable tensor processor 700 reads loop body microcode 724 from the descriptors, filters all instructions that fail condition checking based on condition code 722 received from nested loop sequencer circuit 712, and forwards the resulting microcode (e.g., predicate microcode 726) for the loop body to a trace stage (e.g., pending instruction tracker circuit 718).

For example, in programmable tensor processor 700, inner loop iteration microcode or loop body microcode 724 may include a set of INSTR instructions (e.g., INSTR function "InStr ([ start ], string1, string2, [ compare ])"), where each instruction has a set of associated attributes including predicate conditions, datapath functional unit allocation, relative loop allocation, operation code indicating the type of operation to be performed, a set of input operands, and output operands from one of the register sets.

FIG. 9 illustrates pseudo code for encoding instructions of a functional unit in accordance with one or more embodiments. Fig. 9 illustrates pseudo code or these attributes of the instructions of the inner loop iteration microcode or loop body microcode 724 are represented as pseudo C structures (e.g., as pseudo code, although other encodings may be used).

In one or more embodiments, microcode (e.g., loop body microcode 724) defines the inner loop body instruction set to be executed in a tensor program (e.g., the tensor program of FIG. 8). Each instruction in the microcode (e.g., loop body microcode 724) has an associated loop annotation indicating the relative location of the instruction in the loop body. A compiler in communication with the programmable tensor processor 700 or the user may ensure that instruction loop assignments are not dangerous (e.g., have no resource conflict). This is ensured by either the compiler scheduling instructions or the user manually scheduling instructions. The round robin assignment will depend on the availability of the input operation (the conflict of the output operand of the aforementioned instruction and the resource on the functional unit). In one or more embodiments, multiple instructions may be allocated to the same functional unit (e.g., however, in the same cycle, the assertions do not overlap).

For example, in one or more embodiments, in programmable tensor processor 700, microcode (e.g., loop body microcode 724) is explicitly scheduled by a compiler in communication with programmable tensor processor 700, there is no conflict within a single iteration of the inner loop of the tensor program (e.g., the tensor program of fig. 8), and thus no internal iteration body hazard (e.g., no resource conflict). Microcode (e.g., loop body microcode 724) may explicitly annotate instructions with relative loops and explicitly annotate functional unit allocations.

In one or more embodiments, in programmable tensor processor 700, a microcode program defining an inner loop body (e.g., loop body microcode 724) may be executed in each inner loop iteration. The subset of instructions executed (e.g., predicate microcode 726) may be defined by a set of condition codes (e.g., condition codes 722), which depend on a nested loop iteration count (e.g., loop iteration count 720).

As discussed above, table 1 illustrates a list of predicate codes (e.g., predicate microcode 726) that may be used in a programmable tensor processor 700 that supports a 3-loop hierarchy. Each instruction in the microcode (e.g., loop body microcode 724) may have an associated predicate attribute that indicates a loop condition that the instruction should be executed. Also, as discussed with respect to table 1, programmable tensor processor 700 includes even and odd assertions to avoid register allocation conflicts caused by latency differences between functional units.

Returning now to FIG. 7A, the pending instruction tracker circuit 718 of the programmable tensor processor 700 receives the predicate microcode 726 from the predicate filter circuit 714 and tracks instructions in the 'issue' queue, where the instructions in the issue queue contain the predicate microcode 726 from the predicate filter circuit 714. The instructions at the head of the queue may be issued to the data path circuit 706 (e.g., as an ultralong instruction word bundle as shown in FIG. 7A as "issue instruction bundle to data path" 728). Assertion microcode 726 from assertion filter circuitry 714 may be added to the queue at a location indicated by the microcode instruction relative to the issue slot. If the resulting queue state is not at risk for inner loop iteration, there is no resource conflict, then an instruction (e.g., predicate microcode 726) will only be added to the queue, otherwise, predicate microcode 726 from predicate filter circuit 714 will be suspended (e.g., "resulting queue state" may be the same as "updated queue state" where there is no resource conflict with an instruction already in the queue). Upon removing all dangerous instructions (e.g., resource conflicts) from the queue, the predicate microcode 726 from the predicate filter circuit 714 restarts from the suspension and may be accepted and added to the queue containing instructions to be issued to the datapath circuit 706. For example, the pending instruction tracker circuit 718 maintains a table of scheduled instructions and allocated resources (e.g., registers), issues an instruction bundle from a table header into the data path circuit 706 (e.g., as shown as "issue instruction bundle to data path" 728 of fig. 7A), shifts the table to remove issued instructions, accepts and adds new microcode iterations to the scheduled instruction table, provided that such instructions are not dangerous (e.g., have no resource conflict).

In one or more embodiments, programmable tensor processor 700 may also include a hardware scheduler (e.g., including predicate filter circuit 714) for handling the filtering of loop body microcode 724 based on loop iteration count 720. In one or more embodiments, the hardware scheduler pauses and handles operations that add filtered instructions (e.g., predicate microcode 726) from an entire loop body iteration to the pending instruction queue of the pending instruction tracker circuit 718 (e.g., issue an entire inner loop body per cycle) in the event of inter-iteration body hazards (e.g., resource conflicts).

The data path circuit 706 of the programmable tensor processor 700 will now be described in more detail with respect to fig. 7B. In one or more embodiments, the data path circuit 706 includes one or more functional units for arithmetic functions or for fetching input values (e.g., data streams from the load AGU circuit) from the load AGU circuit (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2)) and one or more register sets storing intermediate results. The data path circuit 706 will pause if the input load value is not available from the load AGU circuit (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2)) or if the storage AGU circuit 708 is not receptive to a new output value.

As illustrated in fig. 7B, example datapath circuitry 706 includes at least four functional unit circuits, such as load Functional Unit (FU) circuits 734 and 736, store FU circuit 738, and Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) circuit 740, and a register bank REGF circuit 742 for storage. In one or more embodiments, as shown in fig. 7C, example data path circuit 706 may also include a multiplier function circuit 744. In one or more embodiments, load FU circuits 734 and 736 of data path circuit 706 may load input operands through load AGU circuits 704 (1), 704 (2). ALU circuitry 740 and multiplier function circuitry 744 of data path circuitry 706 may perform tensor operations on input operands loaded in load FU circuitry 734 and 736 based on instructions 728 received from pending instruction tracker circuitry 718. The tensor operation includes one or more selected from the group of arithmetic operations, look-up table based operations, multiply and multiply-accumulate operations, transpose and shuffle operations, reduce operations, and the like. The storage FU circuit 738 of the data path circuit 706 may store the results of one or more arithmetic and/or logical operations performed in the ALU circuit 740. The results stored in the storage FU circuit 738 of the data path circuit 706 may be transferred to the storage AGU circuit 708 of the programmable tensor processor 700. In the embodiment of fig. 7B, load and store FU circuitry (e.g., 734, 736, 738) streams data to and from load and store AGU circuitry (e.g., 704 (1), 704 (2), 708).

In one or more embodiments, the data path circuit 706 of the programmable tensor processor 700 may include one or more register set reg circuits 742.

In one or more embodiments, intermediate results (e.g., during arithmetic calculations using ALU circuitry 740 of programmable tensor processor 700) may be stored in one or more register file REGF circuitry 742. In one or more embodiments, different types of register sets may be used to store intermediate results. For example, in one or more embodiments, one or more register set REGF circuits 742 may separate different data types. For example, a tensor register set including one or more registers may be used to store intermediate results, with each register storing multidimensional data (e.g., a matrix). As another example, a vector register set including one or more registers may be used to store intermediate results, with each register storing a one-dimensional (1D) array. As yet another example, a scalar register set in which each register stores a zero-dimensional (0D) scalar value may also be used to store intermediate results. For example, a scalar register set stores values applicable to the entire tensor (0D tensor). The per-channel register set stores vectors (1D tensors) broadcast across other dimensions of the operation. For example, in a tensor operation, intermediate results stored in a register set (e.g., register set REGF circuit 742) may be broadcast to multidimensional data (e.g., higher dimensional data) by copying data on a non-primary axis (e.g., secondary axis or higher dimensional axis than the broadcast data, etc.), such as by copying scalar values on two dimensions of the matrix or copying vectors on one of the dimensions of the matrix. In one or more embodiments, the tensor register set temporarily stores intermediate results, thereby avoiding intermediate memory accesses. In one or more embodiments, the vector register may store a 'per channel' quantization parameter or a per channel trained parameter. Also, the vector register may store a reduction result or an index across the maximum of one dimension in a 2D matrix (argax) operation, as is common in AI applications.

The programmable tensor processor 700 can efficiently accelerate AI/ML tensor-based operations while maintaining flexibility. The programmable tensor processor may be efficient, low area, high throughput hardware (e.g., in an edge reasoning processor), or software for performing efficient and flexible tensor operation acceleration in an ANN. The result of the tensor operation performed in the programmable tensor processor 700 may be stored in memory based on the address sequence of the output tensor and may be used as an input to a subsequent ANN layer or may be used as an output of an ANN.

The programmable tensor processor 700 improves system efficiency compared to a conventional processor by: instruction execution using a predefined loop structure and assertions avoids stalls caused by instruction fetch misses by avoiding data-dependent control flows; and avoiding memory load/store suspension by using a predefined sequence of addresses. Avoiding pauses increases the overall performance and energy efficiency of the tensor processor.

Because programmable tensor processor 700 provides an efficient and flexible solution to performing tensor operations in an ANN, the overall efficiency of the ANN may be significantly improved because the ANN will take less time to perform each tensor operation without compromising usage flexibility. For example, the programmable tensor processor 700 may be used to train an ANN in an ANN network or programmable processor, such as a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) device, to accelerate the training process of the ANN in an ANN accelerator or FPGA and in turn to increase the speed of the ANN accelerator and/or FPGA device.
